6. Cost: the selected construction still misses the hurdle

The selected manufacturing estimate includes the newly required foot springs and source/witness hardware.

Manufacturing case	First finished head	Whole-head renewal after 500 services	Complete introduced cost/service
100-head batch	$281.87	$231.87	$1.453
1,000 heads/year	$170.98	$165.98	$1.216
1,000/year, dearer guide-bushing case	$183.36	$178.36	$1.247

The 1,000/year case is a production-volume sensitivity. This user application alone—100 installed heads—does not supply that manufacturing volume.

The model pays for stock, machining, contact-cloth preparation, guides, posts, foot adjustment, pads, springs, locks, drawbar hardware, capture features, assembly, QA and manufacturing rejects. It also includes:

Three spare heads.
An $8,000 shared service tool.
Initial installation and field qualification.
$1,800/year calibration, inspection and maintenance.
Robot occupation, electricity and loaded human exception time.
Cleaning, finite wall-stock allowance and quarantine.
Complete head renewal after 500 accepted services.
Swap labor, waste handling and retirement.

The procurement prices, assembly times, yields and lives are estimating assumptions. In particular, the $20/head matched contact-cloth allowance is unquoted.

A competent practical alternative

The favorable comparison is a floor-supported frame with paid ballast and floor occupation, automated handling, and the same useful fixture load information.

Its introduced cost is:

$1.458/service with free floor space.
$1.708/service with $0.25 per occupied square-metre-day.

The 30% target against the latter is $1.196/service. The selected 1,000/year anchor case exceeds it by about two cents. Against free floor space, the target is $1.021.

This brace is not an exact wall-only substitute. It is a competent whole way to provide the fixture when floor access exists. Its joints and floor response also require qualification; the estimate is not a quotation.

Existing microspine grippers are closer physical comparators, but the reviewed evidence does not supply a matched 500-service purchase. Powered suction and ordinary fastening remain practical alternatives, with their continuous power or surface-restoration differences explicitly retained. Missing matched quotes do not establish an expensive incumbent.
